title: From Nvidia To Amazon, Tech Giants Face Stunning Reversal As Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains
detail:
From Nvidia To Amazon, Tech Giants Face Stunning Reversal As Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains
Matias Civita
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:34 PM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
AMZN
^DJI
NVDA
^IXIC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

U.S. stocks plunged Friday as a deepening sell-off in artificial intelligence companies sent Wall Street toward its worst weekly performance in more than a year, with investors increasingly concerned about technology valuations and the prospect of higher interest rates.

The Nasdaq Composite tumbled more than 5% in late afternoon trading, erasing its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 dropped 3.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.7%. Both the Dow and S&P 500 slipped into correction territory, trading more than 10% below their October record highs.

The S&P 500 was on track for its seventh consecutive losing session, marking its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic rattled global financial markets.

All three major indexes were headed toward their worst weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when President Donald Trump's sweeping tariff announcement triggered a global market downturn. The Dow had already lost approximately 6.2% this week through Thursday's close.

Technology stocks were at the center of Friday's retreat, as the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence developer Anthropic failed to restore confidence in a sector that had powered much of Wall Street's rally this year.

The company behind the Claude chatbot raised approximately $81 billion in its initial public offering on Thursday, surpassing SpaceX to become the largest IPO in history. Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and initially surged more than 30% when trading began. However, the stock surrendered much of those gains before Thursday's closing bell and continued falling Friday.

The disappointing performance compounded concerns about whether the enormous amounts of money flowing into AI companies and infrastructure can generate sufficient returns to justify their valuations.

Semiconductor manufacturers suffered some of Friday's heaviest losses. Nvidia shares plunged approximately 12%, while Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Micron Technology also recorded double-digit declines during the session.

Amazon and Meta Platforms also came under pressure, while AI cloud infrastructure providers CoreWeave and Nebius recorded substantial losses. Companies benefiting indirectly from the expansion of AI infrastructure were also affected. Caterpillar shares declined amid concerns that a slowdown in data center investment could weaken demand for power generation equipment.

The technology rout spread internationally, with Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi both falling more than 5%. Adding to Wall Street's challenges were growing expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again as inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

title: 6 reasons stocks are falling, and what you should do about it
detail:
6 reasons stocks are falling, and what you should do about it
Aimee Picchi
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:15 PM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
ANT
^DJI

The stock market is having its roughest patch since the early days of the pandemic.

Stocks renewed their slide on Friday after tumbling the previous day, with the S&P 500 racking up a seventh consecutive day of losses. The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Here are six factors souring investors' mood, and what experts say you should do about it.

Fears that AI investments might not pay off

Investors are increasingly concerned that the enormous spending on data centers and other infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence may not deliver the hoped-for returns. Anthropic, the first AI lab to go public, has shown rapid revenue growth, but its regulatory filings also point to massive losses — about $104 billion for the first nine months of 2026 alone.

"Those figures explain both the frenzy and the nerves," said Nigel Green, CEO of deVere Group, an investment advisory group. "From here, the market will judge whether the software layer can turn breathtaking growth into lasting profit, and Friday's wobble shows the judging has already begun."

Anti-data center laws could take root

With Democrats set to gain the upper hand in Congress, investors are bracing for new laws that could restrict data center construction when newly elected officials take office in January. Although the shifting political winds aren't expected to halt that buildout, even a modest slowdown could impact the financial results for a range of big tech companies investing heavily in AI.

"The Blue Tidal Wave win and fears about an anti-AI/anti-data center DC" are contributing to the selloff, said Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, in a report on Friday.

The Fed raising interest rates

The Federal Reserve is expected to hike interest rates at its December meeting, as inflation remains well above the central bank's 2% annual target. Raising rates tamps down inflation, but it also makes borrowing more costly, tempering consumer spending and business investment.

"The evidence does not suggest we are on a path back to 2%" without intervention from the central bank, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Austan Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday.

A crackdown on chip exports

The revelation that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a spy for the People's Republic has sparked calls for stricter export rules to China. The ensuing turmoil at Nvidia, including Huang's resignation, has prompted the Commerce Department to move to restrict sales of advanced AI chips to China.

title: Stocks enter correction territory, driven by a deepening tech rout
detail:
Stocks enter correction territory, driven by a deepening tech rout
Aimee Picchi
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 2:08 PM MST 3 min read
^GSPC
^IXIC
^DJI
ANT

Technology stocks plunged on Friday, dimming investor cheer over Anthropic's high-profile IPO this week amid mounting concerns about the health of the artificial intelligence sector.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 1,261 points, or 5.3%, to close at 22,618, the tech-heavy index's second-worst day of 2026 and erasing all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 declined 3.7%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9%.

Both the S&P 500 and Dow entered "correction" territory, meaning the indexes have fallen more than 10% from their most recent highs. The S&P 500 is set for its seventh consecutive day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when the pandemic caused investors to sell in a panic.

Investors are fretting over the value of AI stocks, which drove much of Wall Street's gains earlier this year but are now driving the slide. Microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom led Friday's losses over concerns about a possible slowdown in data center construction and over tighter federal policies on exporting chips outside the U.S.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

The S&P 500's decline into correction territory was largely driven by investors selling AI-related companies, but the underlying U.S. economic and business fundamentals remain solid, said Chris Larkin, managing director of trading and investing at E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, in an email.

"It's impossible to know when any selloff will run its course, but history shows most moves like this don't turn into bear markets —only five of the past 15 corrections from all-time highs since 1983 have done so," he said, referring to when stocks decline 20% or more from the market's most recent peak.

Anthropic can't buck the market

Thursday's big market debut for Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI chatbot, fizzled on Friday, along with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.3% to $88.14, although it remains above its IPO price of $83 per share.

As of early afternoon trading on Friday, Anthropic's stock had fallen about 23% from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive Facebook (now Meta) saw shortly after its May 2012 IPO.

title: If I Could Tell All S&P 500 Investors Just 1 Thing Right Now, It's This
detail:
If I Could Tell All S&P 500 Investors Just 1 Thing Right Now, It's This
David Dierking, The Motley Fool
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 3:05 PM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

At one point in 2025, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) fell 19% below its high. It still finished the year up 16%.

In 2020, the index dropped by nearly 35% during the COVID pandemic. It also closed out the full calendar year with a gain of 16%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

In 2026, stocks are sliding again. Right now, the S&P 500 sits about 6% below its all-time high, but the Nasdaq-100 is down nearly 13%.

I don't tell you this to suggest that U.S. stocks are poised for a rapid recovery like they experienced earlier this decade. It's to tell you that episodes like this are part of the experience when investing in stocks.

If you own the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO), here's the one thing I'd tell you right now. These declines are no doubt painful, but they're the price of admission when accumulating long-term wealth.

Image source: Getty Images.
Stocks often fall 10% on the way to calendar-year gains

Here's an interesting bit of stock market trivia. Since 1980, the average intra-year drop in the S&P 500 has been 14.2%. But despite this, the S&P 500 has produced a positive calendar-year return in 35 of those 46 years.

In other words, market corrections are a normal and regular occurrence for the S&P 500. But so are the recoveries from them. And the fact remains that stocks spend much more time rising than they do falling. The short-term losses are part of the path to long-term gains.

The benefits of doing nothing at all

One of the most underrated moves an investor can make is making no move at all.

When stock prices are falling, many people rush to sell their stocks, fearing that more losses are on the way. They may say something like they're going to wait for things to get "better" before they get back in.

There are a couple of things wrong with that thinking.

First, selling stocks after they've fallen only locks in the loss. It doesn't erase it. Second, stock market rebounds are often well underway by the time investors feel that things have gotten "better."

The sum total of these actions means that a lot of folks lock in the loss, miss out on the rebound, and end up damaging their long-term returns. If the S&P 500's long-term annualized return is around 10%, the average investor usually ends up getting less than that.

That's why the one thing I like to tell investors is: Get used to the stock market's volatility. It's normal and it's a daily occurrence. Corrections of 10% or more are fairly frequent and should be expected from time to time. It's how you handle them that makes the difference. If you can buy and hold instead of giving in to the temptation to sell, you have a better chance of reaching your financial goals.
